title: The First World War: Causes, Events, Consequences
description: The Great War of 1914–1918 — its long-term causes, the assassination at Sarajevo, trench warfare, the great battles, new weapons, the home front, and how and why it ended.

notes.heading: Long-Term Causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism
notes.body: The First World War was not caused by one event; four long-term forces had been pushing Europe towards conflict for decades. **Militarism**: the great powers glorified war and competed in an arms race — Germany and Britain raced to build battleships, and generals drew up detailed war plans that left little room for diplomacy. **Alliances**: Europe split into two armed camps — the **Triple Alliance** (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the **Triple Entente** (Britain, France, Russia) — so a dispute between two countries could drag in all. **Imperialism**: rivalry over colonies in Africa and Asia created friction, as in the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911. **Nationalism**: intense pride in one's nation made peoples eager to prove their strength, while in the Balkans, Slavic nationalists wanted independence from Austria-Hungary — the 'powder keg of Europe'. Together these created a situation of tension and suspicion in which a single spark could start a general war. Historians still debate how far each cause — and especially Germany's role — bears the blame.

notes.heading: Sarajevo and the July Crisis
notes.body: On **28 June 1914**, **Archduke Franz Ferdinand**, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia when he and his wife were shot dead by **Gavrilo Princip**, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to the Black Hand group, which wanted Bosnia to join Serbia. The assassination was the trigger, not the cause, of war. In the **July Crisis** that followed, Austria-Hungary — backed by Germany's 'blank cheque' of support — sent Serbia an ultimatum with deliberately harsh demands. Serbia accepted most but not all of them; Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on **28 July 1914**. The alliance system then pulled the powers in like a chain: Russia mobilised to protect Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia (1 August) and France (3 August); and when Germany invaded neutral **Belgium** to attack France under the **Schlieffen Plan**, Britain declared war on Germany (4 August). Within weeks, a Balkan murder had become a world war — a terrifying demonstration of how alliances and timetables can destroy the space for diplomacy.

notes.heading: Trench Warfare and Life in the Trenches
notes.body: Germany's Schlieffen Plan — a rapid knock-out blow against France before turning on Russia — failed in autumn 1914, and the armies on the **Western Front** dug in. The result was a line of **trenches** stretching more than 700 kilometres from the Belgian coast to Switzerland, barely moving for three years. Between the opposing trenches lay **no man's land**, a shell-torn wasteland of mud, craters and barbed wire. Attacks followed a grim pattern: a massive artillery bombardment (meant to cut the wire and destroy the defenders, but rarely doing either), then infantry went '**over the top**' into machine-gun fire. Life in the trenches was miserable even between battles: soldiers endured mud, rats, lice, the cold, and diseases such as **trench foot**, caused by standing for days in waterlogged boots. Rotation systems gave men periods behind the lines, but the constant shelling caused psychological trauma — **shell shock** — which the army barely understood. Soldiers from Britain, the Empire, France and Germany kept diaries and wrote letters and poetry that survive as powerful primary sources.

notes.heading: Key Battles: Verdun, the Somme, Gallipoli
notes.body: The war's great offensives killed hundreds of thousands for gains measured in metres. At **Verdun** (February–December 1916), Germany attacked intending to 'bleed France white' through attrition; the battle lasted ten months and cost around 700,000 casualties between the two sides, but the line held. The **Battle of the Somme** (July–November 1916) was Britain's great offensive to relieve Verdun: on the first day, **1 July 1916**, the British Army suffered nearly 60,000 casualties, including almost 20,000 dead — the worst day in its history. The battle saw the first use of the **tank** (September 1916) and ended with about a million casualties on both sides for an advance of a few kilometres. At **Gallipoli** (1915), Britain and its allies tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by seizing the Dardanelles strait; the campaign ended in bloody stalemate and evacuation, with heavy losses among Australian and New Zealand (**ANZAC**) troops — an event that shaped those nations' identities. These battles raised questions about generalship that historians still argue over.

notes.heading: New Weapons and Technology
notes.body: The First World War was the first fully industrialised war, and technology outran tactics. The **machine gun** could fire hundreds of rounds a minute and mowed down attacking infantry — a key reason defence dominated and trenches formed. **Artillery** caused the majority of all casualties; shellfire churned battlefields into mud. **Poison gas** — chlorine (1915) and later mustard gas — was first used by Germany at Ypres; it caused terror and horrific injuries, though gas masks soon limited its effect. The **tank**, used by Britain from 1916, could cross trenches and crush barbed wire, but early models were slow and unreliable; it only proved decisive in 1918. **Aircraft** evolved from reconnaissance spotters to fighters and bombers. At sea, German **U-boats** (submarines) waged unrestricted warfare on Allied shipping, sinking ships such as the liner *Lusitania* (1915, with the loss of 1,198 lives) and nearly starving Britain in 1917 — but also helping bring the **United States** into the war. Each new weapon was eventually answered by a countermeasure, feeding the stalemate.

notes.heading: The Home Front
notes.body: This was **total war**: whole economies and societies were mobilised, blurring the line between soldier and civilian. In Britain, the Defence of the Realm Act (**DORA**, 1914) gave the government sweeping powers over industry, the press and daily life. **Conscription** (from 1916) compelled men into the army, while millions of **women** took jobs in munitions factories, on farms and in transport — work that transformed attitudes and helped women over 30 win the vote in 1918. **Propaganda** posters and censored news sustained morale and demonised the enemy; '**conscientious objectors**' who refused to fight on moral grounds faced imprisonment or scorn. As U-boats attacked food imports, Britain introduced voluntary and then compulsory **rationing** (1918). Civilians also faced direct attack from Zeppelin and bomber raids. All the warring powers experienced similar strains; in Germany the Allied **blockade** caused the desperate 'turnip winter' of 1916–17. War on the home front decided the war as much as battles did: victory went to the side whose economy and society could endure longest.

notes.heading: Why Germany Lost: The Armistice and Consequences
notes.body: In March 1918, with Russia defeated and out of the war, Germany hurled its reserves into the **Spring Offensive**, gambling on victory before American troops arrived in force. The attack gained ground but exhausted itself. The Allies, now strengthened by over a million fresh **American soldiers** and using tanks and aircraft in combined attacks, struck back in the **Hundred Days Offensive** (August–November 1918), breaking the German lines. Germany's allies collapsed, the navy mutinied, revolution spread, and **Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated** on 9 November. At 11 a.m. on **11 November 1918**, the **armistice** — a ceasefire — came into force; the Great War was over. Germany lost because it could not win a long war of attrition against enemies with greater combined resources, more men, and control of the seas. The consequences were immense: about 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians were dead; four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman) had collapsed; and the **Treaty of Versailles** (1919) imposed harsh terms on Germany whose bitterness helped cause the Second World War just twenty years later.

flashcards.definition: The glorification of military power and readiness for war — a long-term cause of WWI, seen in the Anglo-German naval arms race.
flashcards.example: Britain and Germany competing to build ever more Dreadnought battleships before 1914.

flashcards.definition: The alliance of Britain, France and Russia, formed between 1894 and 1907, which faced the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy.
flashcards.example: When Germany attacked France in 1914, the Entente commitments drew in Russia and Britain.

flashcards.definition: Archduke and heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 — the trigger for the First World War.
flashcards.example: His killer, Gavrilo Princip, was a Bosnian Serb nationalist who wanted Bosnia to join Serbia.

flashcards.definition: Germany's 1914 war plan: knock France out quickly by attacking through Belgium, then turn east to fight Russia. Its failure led to trench stalemate.
flashcards.example: Invading neutral Belgium brought Britain into the war against Germany in August 1914.

flashcards.definition: The shell-torn strip of mud, craters and barbed wire between the opposing trench lines on the Western Front.
flashcards.example: Soldiers ordered 'over the top' had to cross no man's land under machine-gun fire.

flashcards.definition: A crippling condition caused by standing for days in cold, waterlogged trenches; untreated, it could lead to gangrene and amputation.
flashcards.example: Soldiers were ordered to keep boots dry and rub whale oil into their feet to prevent it.

flashcards.definition: The British offensive of July–November 1916; nearly 60,000 British casualties on the first day (1 July) and about a million in total, for a few kilometres of ground.
flashcards.example: The Somme saw the first use of the tank in September 1916.

flashcards.definition: The ten-month 1916 battle in which Germany tried to 'bleed France white' through attrition; around 700,000 casualties in total.
flashcards.example: Verdun became a symbol of French determination — 'They shall not pass.'

flashcards.definition: The failed 1915 Allied campaign to seize the Dardanelles from the Ottoman Empire, ending in evacuation after heavy losses.
flashcards.example: ANZAC troops from Australia and New Zealand suffered heavily, shaping both nations' identities.

flashcards.definition: A German submarine. Unrestricted U-boat warfare against merchant shipping nearly starved Britain but helped bring the USA into the war in 1917.
flashcards.example: A U-boat sank the liner Lusitania in 1915, killing 1,198 people including 128 Americans.

flashcards.definition: A war in which entire societies and economies are mobilised and civilians become participants and targets, blurring the line with the battlefield.
flashcards.example: British women worked in munitions factories while rationing and propaganda regulated civilian life.

flashcards.definition: The ceasefire that ended the fighting on the Western Front at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.
flashcards.example: Armistice Day, 11 November, is still marked each year as Remembrance Day.

questions.stem: Which four long-term causes are usually grouped together to explain the outbreak of the First World War?
choices: Monarchy, aristocracy, industry and nationalism
Militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism
Trade, travel, technology and treaties
Religion, revolution, railways and radar
questions.explanation: Historians use militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism to explain the rising tension before 1914: the arms race, the two alliance blocs, colonial rivalry and aggressive national pride made a general war increasingly likely.

questions.stem: Why did the alliance system make a European war more likely?
choices: Alliances forced countries to disarm their armies
Alliances meant countries had to hold regular elections
A conflict between two countries could pull in their allies, turning a small dispute into a continent-wide war
Alliances prevented any country from building battleships
questions.explanation: The Triple Alliance and Triple Entente bound the powers to support their partners. In July 1914 a dispute between Austria-Hungary and Serbia dragged in Russia, Germany, France and Britain within a single week.

questions.stem: Who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo in June 1914, and why?
choices: Kaiser Wilhelm II, to start a German war of conquest
Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist who wanted Bosnia to break from Austria-Hungary and join Serbia
Tsar Nicholas II, to protect Russian influence in Serbia
A British spy, to bring Britain into the war
questions.explanation: Princip, linked to the Black Hand nationalist group, shot the Archduke because he wanted Bosnian independence from Austria-Hungary and union with Serbia. The assassination was the trigger that the July Crisis turned into war.

questions.stem: How did the Schlieffen Plan help turn the 1914 crisis into a world war?
choices: It required Germany to invade neutral Belgium to attack France, which brought Britain into the war
It was a peace plan rejected by France
It allied Germany with the United States
It called for the immediate invasion of Britain
questions.explanation: Germany's plan to beat France quickly demanded an advance through Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed. Britain therefore declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, widening the conflict into a global struggle involving empires worldwide.

choices: The area between the opposing trench lines, a wasteland of mud, craters and barbed wire
Land that no country claimed in Africa
The zone behind the front where only officers could go
Neutral territory ruled by the Red Cross
questions.explanation: No man's land separated the enemy trench systems. Attacking infantry had to cross it in the open, exposed to machine guns and artillery — one reason offensives cost so many lives for so little ground.

questions.stem: Why did trench warfare produce a stalemate on the Western Front?
choices: Both sides ran out of ammunition by 1915
Soldiers on both sides refused to fight
Defensive weapons — machine guns, artillery and barbed wire — were stronger than attack, so offensives failed and neither side could break through
The trenches were too far apart for anyone to attack
questions.explanation: Defence dominated: machine guns and artillery slaughtered attackers crossing no man's land, and defenders could rush reserves by rail to any breakthrough. Until 1918, technology and tactics favoured holding ground over taking it.

questions.stem: What happened on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916?
choices: Germany surrendered to the Allies
The British Army suffered nearly 60,000 casualties — the worst single day in its history
The tank won a decisive victory
The war ended with an armistice
questions.explanation: After a week-long bombardment that failed to destroy German defences, British infantry attacked and suffered around 57,000 casualties, almost 20,000 of them killed. The Somme became a symbol of the war's slaughter and of debates over its generals.

questions.stem: What was Germany's aim at the Battle of Verdun in 1916?
choices: To capture Paris in a single week
To 'bleed France white' — to inflict such heavy casualties through attrition that France could not fight on
To test the first tanks in battle
To force Britain to withdraw from Gallipoli
questions.explanation: The German plan at Verdun was attrition: attack a fortress the French would defend at all costs and destroy their army in the process. After ten months and some 700,000 casualties on both sides, the line had barely moved.

questions.stem: Which weapon, first used by Britain at the Somme in September 1916, was designed to cross trenches and crush barbed wire?
choices: The machine gun
Poison gas
The fighter aircraft
The tank
questions.explanation: The tank was built to break the trench deadlock by crossing mud, wire and trenches under armour. Early tanks were slow and unreliable, but by 1918 they played a real part in the Allied advance.

questions.stem: Why did Germany's use of unrestricted submarine warfare backfire?
choices: U-boats could not sink merchant ships
Sinking neutral and civilian ships outraged the United States and helped bring it into the war against Germany in 1917
Submarines were only useful for exploration
Britain had no ships left to sink
questions.explanation: U-boats came close to starving Britain, but sinking ships like the Lusitania and attacking neutral shipping pushed the USA towards war. Germany gambled on winning before American power counted — and lost the gamble.

questions.stem: Which of these is the clearest example of the First World War as a 'total war'?
choices: Only professional soldiers were affected by the fighting
Women worked in munitions factories, food was rationed, and the government controlled industry and information
Civilians were forbidden to read newspapers
Battles were fought far from any town
questions.explanation: Total war mobilised entire societies: DORA gave Britain's government sweeping powers, women filled industrial jobs, rationing managed food, and propaganda and censorship shaped opinion. Civilian effort became as decisive as the armies.

questions.stem: What long-term political consequence did women's war work help bring about in Britain?
choices: Women were banned from factory work after the war
Women over 30 won the right to vote in 1918
Women were conscripted into the army from 1916
No change — attitudes stayed exactly the same
questions.explanation: Millions of women proved their capability in munitions, farming and transport. In 1918 the Representation of the People Act gave the vote to women over 30 — the start of political equality, completed in 1928.

questions.stem: When did the First World War end on the Western Front?
choices: 28 June 1914, with the Sarajevo assassination
1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme
At 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918, when the armistice came into force
28 June 1919, with the Treaty of Versailles
questions.explanation: The fighting ended with the armistice at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918. The Treaty of Versailles, signed in June 1919, was the peace settlement that followed, not the end of the fighting.

questions.stem: Why did the German Spring Offensive of March 1918 ultimately fail?
choices: Germany attacked Russia instead of France
The offensive gained ground but exhausted Germany's last reserves, and the Allies counter-attacked with fresh American troops, tanks and aircraft
British civilians refused to support the war
Winter snow stopped all fighting until 1919
questions.explanation: Germany gambled on victory before US forces arrived in strength. The offensive advanced but outran its supplies and used up its best troops; the Allied Hundred Days counter-offensive, powered by a million fresh Americans and combined arms, then broke the German army.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the Treaty of Versailles was the most important consequence of the First World War. Which evidence best supports this judgement?
choices: The treaty ended all wars in Europe permanently
Its harsh terms bred bitterness in Germany that Hitler later exploited, making it a long-term cause of the Second World War
The treaty had no effect on Germany
The treaty was signed before the war began
questions.explanation: Versailles (1919) imposed heavy reparations, lost territory and a 'war guilt' clause on Germany. The resentment it created was exploited by the Nazis, linking the peace settlement directly to the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 — a consequence of enormous significance.
